teaser.text: Advanced Micro Devices, or AMD, makes the chips and supporting technology that turn computers into useful machines. Its business is a chain: customers choose AMD’s designs, specialist manufacturers build them, and AMD collects the difference after paying for engineering and production.

blocks.heading: What has to go right, and what could go wrong for AMD?

paragraphs.text: The bear case uses $11,000M, then $9,500M, before recovering to $12,000M. It assumes delayed systems, weaker adoption and cash-heavy commitments. The bull case uses $23,000M, then $33,000M and $42,000M. It requires on-time production, repeat paid deployments and successful ROCm adoption.

blocks.heading: How much cash does AMD really make?

paragraphs.text: Operating cash from continuing operations was US$6,493 million in 2025. After capital spending of US$974 million, free cash flow was US$5,519 million, or 15.9% of revenue. That recovered from US$2,405 million in 2024 and US$1,121 million in 2023. Acquisition proceeds and payments belong elsewhere in the cash-flow statement, so they do not represent recurring operating conversion.

Stock-based pay creates another gap between accounting profit and owner economics. AMD added the expense back to operating cash because issuing shares uses no cash immediately. Deducting the US$1,638 million expense from free cash flow leaves US$3,881 million. That is an analytical allowance for the cost borne by shareholders, not a separate cash payment. It produces real free cash flow per share of US$2.37.

blocks.heading: What has AMD guided for the next quarter?

paragraphs.text: For the quarter to September 2026, management guides revenue to $12,700–$13,300 million. It guides to a 56.0% non-GAAP gross margin. Management expects Data Center revenue growth well over 100% in 2027.

blocks.heading: Has AMD kept its past promises?

paragraphs.text: AMD did complete its stated plan to retain ZT’s design expertise and sell manufacturing; the harder test is whether future growth and rewards produce enough cash and per-share value to justify their cost.

blocks.heading: What do AMD's last eight quarters show?

paragraphs.text: Operating cash was US$2,366 million. After US$808 million of capital spending, calculated free cash flow was US$1,558 million, against US$1,180 million a year earlier. Cash conversion improved, but capital spending grew faster than sales. The quarter shows a stronger AMD led by data-center demand, alongside weaker Gaming and greater cash requirements; several more quarters must show whether that balance persists.

blocks.heading: What should investors watch in AMD's next results?

paragraphs.text: The next results must show whether Helios shipments are becoming repeatable while export permissions remain volatile.

AMD’s next reporting event is scheduled for November 3, 2026. The September checkpoint is initial delivery to manufacturing partners near the end of Q3; the stronger test is Q4 system production and customer deployment. Components leaving a factory do not prove that a usable system has reached production.
